segments.source: Public budgets require choices under limited resources. A transparent model separates costs, benefits, and mandatory obligations.
A town has a budget of 21 units. Projects (cost, benefit): tree planting=(5,7); bridge repair=(6,9); library books=(3,4); drainage=(5,8).
Choose a subset whose total cost does not exceed the budget. Maximize total benefit. If a mandatory project is stated, every feasible plan must include it.
Which set of projects gives the greatest total benefit while satisfying every constraint?

1. Budget limit is 21. 2. Evaluate feasible combinations (and keep the mandatory project if any). 3. The best feasible combination has cost 19 and benefit 28: ['tree planting', 'bridge repair', 'library books', 'drainage']. 4. No higher-benefit feasible combination exists under the stated costs.
Choose tree planting, bridge repair, library books, drainage; cost 19, benefit 28.
Optimization means comparing feasible alternatives under an explicit objective, not simply choosing the cheapest item.
0/1 knapsack with optional mandatory-item constraint; maximize benefit subject to total cost ≤ budget.

Public budgets require choices under limited resources. A transparent model separates costs, benefits, and mandatory obligations.
A town has a budget of 22 units. Projects (cost, benefit): park=(4,5); bridge repair=(6,9); library books=(3,4); drainage=(5,8). Safety rule: bridge repair must be included.
Choose a subset whose total cost does not exceed the budget. Maximize total benefit. If a mandatory project is stated, every feasible plan must include it.
Which set of projects gives the greatest total benefit while satisfying every constraint?

Choose park, bridge repair, library books, drainage; cost 18, benefit 26.

Problem 871. Pairwise collective choice: Park versus Library
Group preferences can be aggregated in different ways. Pairwise majority asks a specific question about two options at a time.

Three public projects are considered: Park, Library, Sports Hall. Voter groups and rankings: 4 voters rank Park>Library>Sports Hall; 7 voters rank Library>Sports Hall>Park; 2 voters rank Sports Hall>Park>Library. Use pairwise majority: compare two options at a time; each voter supports the one ranked higher.
For a pairwise contest, count how many voters prefer each of the two options. Ignore the third option for that comparison.
In a pairwise vote between Park and Library, which option wins?
1. For each group, check whether Park or Library is ranked higher. 2. Totals: Park=6, Library=7. 3. Therefore the result is Library.
A collective decision rule must be explicit; different rules can summarize the same rankings differently.
Preference rankings; for pair (a,b), sum weights of voters ranking a>b versus b>a.

Part B — New and mixed reasoning domains
Map scale links a model to the real world through proportional reasoning.
A map has scale 1:10000. The measured map distance between two points is 6 cm. Rule: 1 cm on the map represents 10000 cm in reality; 100,000 cm = 1 km.
Multiply map length by the scale denominator, then convert units. A scale is a ratio, not an added distance.
What is the real straight-line distance in kilometres?
Scale problems are ratio problems: keep units explicit and conversion becomes mechanical.
Proportion d_real=d_map×denominator, followed by unit conversion.
